analysis.one_liner: Required escort vessels, licensed pilots, and spill-response equipment for oil tankers in Prince William Sound.
analysis.headline: The bill, written after the Exxon Valdez spill, won committee approval on July 31, 1989 with 12 cosponsors from both parties, but the House passed a broader oil pollution bill instead and it never got a vote of its own.
analysis.plain_summary: Written as a direct response to the Exxon Valdez oil spill of March 24, 1989, this bill would have required every tanker leaving the Port of Valdez to travel with an escort vessel, an additional Alaska-licensed pilot, and enough onboard boom and pumps to contain a leak. It would have prepositioned cleanup equipment in Valdez and Cordova, stationed a trained response team able to handle a 200,000-barrel spill, run regular spill drills, taken licenses away from mariners who abuse alcohol, and funded at least $5 million a year in monitoring of damage to Alaska fisheries.
analysis.who_benefits: Alaska's coastal communities and the fishing and fish-farming operations around Prince William Sound, whose fisheries and shorelines the bill was designed to shield from a repeat of the Exxon Valdez disaster. The bill also gave them training in spill containment and paid for ongoing monitoring of damage to living marine resources.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Alaska fishing towns and coastal communities

how_it_helps.text: Tankers carrying oil from the Trans-Alaska Pipeline through Prince William Sound would have to be escorted by a towing vessel and navigated with an additional Alaska-licensed pilot between Valdez and a point south of Bligh Reef — the reef the Exxon Valdez struck.

Tankers would have to carry heavy-duty boom and equipment able to encircle the vessel at 100 yards, and cleanup gear would be prepositioned at Valdez, Cordova and other locations, with a standing response team sized for a 200,000-barrel spill and drills at least twice a year.

The amended version gave a single federal authority — the Secretary of Transportation — the power to direct all federal, state, and private containment and cleanup activities, ending the lack of centralized authority Congress found had hindered the Exxon Valdez response, and made responsible parties liable for the actual costs.

The Coast Guard could suspend or revoke the licenses of mariners determined to be current or chronic abusers of alcohol, and check their driving records through the National Driver Register — a response to the human failures behind the grounding.

Commerce would spend at least $5 million a year from 1990 through 1992 assessing and monitoring damage to Alaska's living marine resources from the spill, with the money recoverable whenever possible from the Exxon Valdez's owner or operator.
Commercial fishermen and fish cultivators would receive training in oil spill containment and recovery techniques, preparing the people whose livelihoods depend on the Sound to help protect it.

analysis.who_pays: Oil tanker operators and the companies shipping crude through the Trans-Alaska Pipeline would bear the compliance costs — escort vessels, a second pilot, onboard spill equipment — plus liability for federal cleanup costs and, where possible, repayment of the monitoring money. Federal appropriations would front the $5 million a year in monitoring and $8 million in authorized research and studies until costs were recovered.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil tanker operators and Alaska Pipeline shippers

drawbacks.text: The bill was strictly regional: its requirements covered only Alaska's 'Arctic waters,' leaving tanker routes and coastlines elsewhere in the country without escort, pilotage, or response requirements — a gap a national oil pollution law would later fill.

The compliance costs are real: round-the-clock escort vessels, a second state-licensed pilot on every transit, and carrying containment equipment large enough to encircle a supertanker all add cost to every load of crude shipped out of Valdez, costs that flow into oil shipping rates.

As introduced, the license provisions were blunt — revoking a mariner's credentials for any alcohol-related conviction within the previous ten years; the committee's amended version narrowed this to suspend or revoke licenses of current or chronic abusers of alcohol, a softer standard.
The fisheries monitoring money comes out of regular appropriations first and is only recovered from the spiller 'whenever possible,' so taxpayers front the cost if recovery falls short.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: On its own terms the bill was a modest, well-targeted fix: a few million dollars a year in monitoring and research, and compliance costs on shippers using one of the busiest oil ports in the country, weighed against protecting one of America's richest fisheries from a repeat of a spill Congress itself called an 'economic and ecological disaster of major proportions.' Its main weakness was narrowness — it fixed Alaska but left the rest of the coast exposed — which is part of why the House preferred a comprehensive oil pollution bill instead.

outcome.mechanism: The House folded the effort into a bigger oil pollution bill, H.R. 1465, which became the Oil Pollution Act of 1990, and this narrower Alaska-only bill never got a floor vote of its own.

narrative.text: The Exxon Valdez grounded on Bligh Reef in Prince William Sound on March 24, 1989. Congress's findings in the bill itself called the spill an 'economic and ecological disaster of major proportions,' said the response had been hindered by lack of centralized authority, and called the approved contingency plan for the Sound 'wholly inadequate.'
Rep. Don Young of Alaska introduced the bill on April 27, 1989, one month after the spill, and it drew 12 cosponsors split evenly between six Democrats and six Republicans.
Subcommittees held hearings in May 1989, and the House Merchant Marine and Fisheries Committee amended the bill and reported it to the House on July 31, 1989 as H. Rept. 101-200, Part I.

Instead of taking up the narrow Alaska bill, the House moved on the broader oil pollution bill H.R. 1465 — the bill's action record closes on November 9, 1989 with 'See H.R.1465' — and H.R. 2158 never received a vote on the House floor.

The committee version of H.R. 2158 already contained the core ideas that defined the oil pollution debate that followed: stronger tanker navigation requirements in the Sound, centralized federal authority over spill response, responsible-party liability for costs, and money to monitor damage to fisheries.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coastal communities and the fishing industry effectively came out ahead: the substance they wanted was enacted through the bigger, stronger national oil pollution law rather than a regional bill, while tanker operators faced stricter national requirements instead of Alaska-only ones. No one lost much by this bill dying, since its provisions were largely carried forward in the comprehensive legislation.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Coastal communities, via the bigger oil pollution law

for.name: Don Young
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill one month after the Exxon Valdez spill and guided it through subcommittee and committee.

for.name: Walter B. Jones
for.role: Chair, House Committee on Merchant Marine and Fisheries
for.what_they_did: His committee held hearings, amended the bill, ordered it reported on June 21, and reported it to the House on July 31, 1989 (H. Rept. 101-200, Part I).

for.name: 12 House cosponsors — 6 Democrats and 6 Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, splitting evenly across party lines.

against.name: House majority leadership
against.what_they_did: Chose to advance the comprehensive oil pollution bill H.R. 1465 as the House's vehicle rather than this narrower Alaska-only bill, leaving H.R. 2158 without a floor vote.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had no recorded floor vote, but its 12 cosponsors split evenly — 6 Democrats and 6 Republicans — behind a Republican sponsor, and the Democratic-led Merchant Marine and Fisheries Committee reported it; the choice of a different vehicle was not fought along party lines on the record.

industries.industry: Oil tanker operators and Alaska Pipeline shippers
industries.note: The bill required escort vessels, an extra Alaska-licensed pilot, and onboard containment gear for every tanker transit out of Valdez, and made responsible parties liable for cleanup and monitoring costs. These are exactly the costs the industry would otherwise avoid, and the Exxon Valdez spill showed who bears them when the industry doesn't pay upfront.

industries.industry: Alaska commercial fishing and fish farming
industries.note: The bill's prepositioned equipment, response teams sized for a 200,000-barrel spill, and $5 million a year in fisheries damage monitoring all exist to protect the Sound's fishery — the livelihood the spill devastated. Fish cultivators would also get spill-response training.

industries.industry: Oil spill response and marine safety contractors
industries.note: Mandated prepositioned cleanup equipment, new radar sites for the Vessel Traffic System, standing response teams, and twice-yearly drills create sustained demand for spill-response gear, personnel, and training. The public benefit and the contractors' revenue run together here.
The bill directed Commerce to recover the cost of fisheries damage assessments and monitoring from the Exxon Valdez's owner or operator whenever possible, adding to the company's spill tab.
